name: Design an Incident Management Platform
intent: Turn a flood of alerts into a handful of incidents, get the right person awake within minutes, keep customers informed, and keep all of it working on the day everything else is on fire.
codeTitle: alert grouping, escalation paging and status fan-out
finalIntro: One serious outage, from the first alert to a status update in every subscriber's inbox.
prompt: Design the incident management platform for a company with 800 engineers and 200,000 status page subscribers. Monitoring tools raise alerts, and the platform must declare incidents with a severity, page the on-call engineer and escalate if nobody answers, assign a commander and a communications lead, record a timeline, publish status page updates to subscribers, offer runbooks and automation, and track postmortems and their action items. It must keep working when the company's main infrastructure is down.
functional: Receive alerts from many monitoring tools and group them into incidents with a severity
Page the on-call engineer, escalate when nobody acknowledges, and assign roles such as commander and communications lead
Record a timeline of everything that happens in an incident
Publish status page updates and send them to subscribers by email, SMS and webhook
Attach runbooks to alerts and run safe automated actions such as a rollback
Write postmortems from the timeline and track their action items until they are done
nonFunctional: A page reaches a phone within 30 seconds of the alert reaching the platform
The platform is available when the services it watches are down, so it is more reliable than anything it monitors
A status update reaches 200,000 subscribers within a few minutes
No alert is lost, and no engineer is paged twice for the same problem
The timeline is complete, ordered and cannot be edited afterwards
Everything works during an alert storm of thousands of alerts in a minute

firstAttempt.text: Each monitoring tool sends an email to a mailing list, someone opens a chat room and a shared document, and a person on call is phoned by hand if nobody replies. Status updates are posted to the status page by whoever remembers, and the lessons are written up later from memory.
limits: One failure raises hundreds of alerts, and every one of them interrupts someone
Nobody knows who owns the problem, so several people debug the same thing and none talks to customers
An email to a sleeping engineer is not a page, and nothing escalates when it goes unread
The record of what happened is scattered over chat, memory and the shell history
If the chat tool, the mail system or the status page runs in the same cloud as the outage, they fail together with the thing they are meant to report on

steps.title: Group alerts into incidents with a severity
steps.problem: A single failed database can raise five hundred alerts from fifty services in a minute. Paging someone for each one buries the real problem and wears out the people who must solve it.
steps.fix: All monitoring tools send alerts to one intake with a common shape: a service, a fingerprint of the problem, a severity and a time. The incident engine groups alerts that share a service or a dependency and arrive close together into one incident. A repeated alert only increments a counter on the open incident. The incident takes the worst severity of its alerts, where severity 1 means customers are badly hurt right now and severity 3 means a degraded internal tool. Declaring is also possible by hand, from a chat command, so a human who notices something before the monitoring does can start one in seconds.
steps.tradeoff: One incident replaces hundreds of pages, and severity decides who is woken up and how loudly. Grouping that is too eager merges two unrelated problems into one, so the engine groups by service first and lets a responder split or merge incidents. Too little grouping brings the storm back.

steps.title: Page the on-call engineer and escalate until someone answers
steps.problem: An alert in a mailbox does not wake anybody. Someone must be reached on a phone, and if that person is asleep, out of coverage or has lost their phone, the problem must move on to the next person without a human having to notice.
steps.fix: Each team has an on-call schedule and an escalation policy: the primary is paged by push notification first, then by SMS and a voice call, and if there is no acknowledgement within five minutes the secondary is paged, then the manager. Every page is a durable job on a queue with a deadline, so a crash of the pager does not lose it. The first person to acknowledge becomes the incident commander, who coordinates but does not debug. For serious incidents the engine also pages a communications lead who owns what customers are told, and a scribe role if the team uses one. Acknowledging stops the escalation timer, and a person can hand the commander role to another with one action.
steps.tradeoff: A problem always reaches a human, and the roles stop everyone from doing everything. It costs a schedule that must be kept up to date, and a rule that is too eager wakes the manager for a slow phone. Acknowledgement windows are a balance between waking too many people and waiting too long.

steps.title: Capture an append-only timeline and learn from it
steps.problem: In the heat of an outage nobody writes things down, and afterwards the sequence of events and decisions is argued about from memory. Lessons that are not recorded are learned again at the next outage.
steps.fix: Every event is appended to a timeline log as an immutable entry with a sequence number: alerts, pages and acknowledgements, role changes, severity changes, status updates, and every command run by the automation. A chat bridge adds messages from the incident channel and lets people mark one as a decision or a finding with a short command. Corrections are new entries, never edits. After the incident the postmortem is created from the timeline with the facts pre-filled, so people spend time on causes instead of reconstruction. Action items are tracked as tickets with an owner and a due date, reviewed weekly, and an overdue one is escalated to the owner's manager.
steps.tradeoff: The record is complete, ordered and trustworthy, and a postmortem starts with facts. The log grows with every message, so old incidents are moved to cheap storage, and a blameless culture must come with it, otherwise people stop recording what they did.

steps.title: Fan out status page updates to subscribers
steps.problem: Customers want to hear from you, not guess. One status update must reach 200,000 people by email, SMS and webhook, within minutes, while the same people are refreshing the page and the senders are at their limits.
steps.fix: The communications lead writes one update, which is stored and published to the status page as a static page behind a CDN. A fan-out job then splits the subscriber list into batches of a few hundred and puts them on a queue. Workers send each message through email, SMS and webhook providers, with a key made from the update and the subscriber so that a retry never creates a second message. Failures are retried with backoff, and a provider that keeps failing is skipped for a while in favour of another. Subscribers can choose components and severity levels, so a customer only hears about what affects them.
steps.tradeoff: Updates reach everyone quickly and nobody gets the same message twice. Provider limits and delivery delays are real, so the page is the source of truth and messages are best effort. A message sent to the wrong audience is hard to take back, so the update goes through a preview and a single approver for severity 1.

steps.title: Attach runbooks and safe automation
steps.problem: At three in the morning a tired engineer should not have to search a wiki for the right steps, and some fixes, such as restarting a service or rolling back a release, are the same every time.
steps.fix: Each alert type links to a runbook, which the incident page shows as soon as the incident is declared, together with recent deploys and the owner of the service. Runbook steps that are safe and repeatable become actions that a responder can start with a button: roll back the last release, drain a region, scale a service, toggle a feature flag. The runner executes each action with the responder's identity, checks permissions, asks for a confirmation on dangerous ones, limits how often it can be repeated, and writes the action and its result to the timeline. Some well-understood alerts run their action automatically after a delay, and page a human if it does not help.
steps.tradeoff: Common problems get fixed in seconds, and every action is recorded. Automation can also make an incident worse at machine speed, so it needs limits, dry runs and a global stop, and runbooks decay when nobody reviews them, so each one has an owner and a last-verified date.

steps.title: Keep the platform alive when everything else is down
steps.problem: The platform is most needed when the main infrastructure is failing. If it runs in the same region, uses the same login, the same DNS and the same chat tool, it falls over together with the outage it should report.
steps.fix: Run it apart: in a separate cloud account or even another provider, with its own database, own DNS and own login that does not depend on the company identity system. Keep a standby site with a continuously replicated copy of the incident store and timeline, and a documented, tested way to switch to it. The pager has paths that do not depend on the internal network, including SMS and voice providers from two vendors and a printed phone tree as the last resort. The status page is a static site on a different CDN and domain, so it keeps serving when the main site is gone. The platform keeps its dependencies few and simple, and it is tested by regular game days where the main infrastructure is deliberately turned off.
steps.tradeoff: The platform works at the moment it is needed. It costs a second environment that must be kept in step, and small things such as a certificate that expires or a separate login that nobody uses are the usual cause of failure, so the standby is exercised often instead of trusted.

failures.scenario: The primary on-call engineer does not answer
failures.impact: The incident has no owner while customers are affected, and each minute adds to the damage.
failures.answer: The escalation timer expires after five minutes and the secondary is paged, then the manager. If the whole chain stays silent, the platform pages the entire team and raises a visible alarm in the operations channel. The unanswered page is recorded in the timeline, and the schedule is reviewed afterwards to find out why the phone was not reached.

failures.scenario: An alert storm sends thousands of alerts per minute
failures.impact: The intake is overloaded and the real signal is lost among duplicates, or the pager starts calling people repeatedly.
failures.answer: Intake accepts alerts quickly into a queue and answers at once. Duplicates are merged by fingerprint into a counter on the open incident, and the pager sends one page per incident, not per alert. If the queue grows beyond a limit the platform sheds the lowest severities first and keeps the highest, and a single message tells the commander that alerts are being summarised.

failures.scenario: The region that hosts the platform goes down with the outage
failures.impact: Nobody can open incidents, the pager stops, and the status page is gone just when customers look for it.
failures.answer: The platform's own health check, run from a third place, notices and switches traffic to the standby site, which has a replicated copy of open incidents and the schedule. Paging continues over providers that do not depend on the failed region, and the static status page on another CDN keeps serving. Entries made during the switch are merged into the timeline afterwards, in sequence order.

failures.scenario: An automated action makes the incident worse
failures.impact: A rollback script restarts every instance at once, and a partial outage becomes a full one.
failures.answer: Actions run in small steps with a wait and a health check between them, and stop by themselves when the error rate rises. A global switch disables all automation immediately, and every action is in the timeline with its result so the commander sees what was done. After the incident the action gets a smaller blast radius and a test before it is allowed to run unattended.

alternatives.title: Build or buy

options.name: Buy a hosted incident product
options.pro: Mature paging, phone reliability and integrations from day one
options.con: Cost grows with seats, and you depend on one vendor for the most critical path

options.name: Build everything yourself
options.pro: Full control and tight fit with internal tools
options.con: Paging reliability and phone carrier relations are hard, and the team must maintain a system that nobody notices until it breaks

options.name: Buy paging, build the workflow
options.pro: The hard, carrier-facing part is rented and the company specific process is yours
options.con: Two systems to integrate and keep in step

alternatives.pick: Rent the paging and phone delivery, build the incident workflow and the timeline around it, and keep an independent second path for paging.

alternatives.title: Where the platform runs

options.name: Inside the main cloud and region
options.pro: Simple, cheap and uses the same tools and login as everything else
options.con: Fails together with the outage it should manage

options.name: A separate cloud account in another region
options.pro: Survives a regional failure while keeping most tooling
options.con: Still shares the provider and sometimes the identity system

options.name: A different provider with its own login and DNS
options.pro: Independent of the main infrastructure in every layer
options.con: A second environment to run, patch and test

alternatives.pick: A different provider for the pager and the status page at least, with a replicated standby for the rest.

alternatives.title: How a status update reaches people

options.name: Page only
options.con: Customers have to come and look

options.name: Page plus email and webhook
options.pro: Reaches most subscribers at low cost, and machines can react
options.con: Delivery is best effort and spam filters delay it

options.name: Add SMS and voice
options.pro: Reaches people who are away from a computer
options.con: Costs money per message and has rate limits, so it is used for severity 1 only

alternatives.pick: Page plus email and webhook for everyone, and SMS for those who opt in for serious incidents.

alternatives.title: How to group alerts

options.name: By service and time window
options.con: Misses a shared dependency that causes alerts in many services

options.name: By a service dependency map
options.pro: Finds the root service and pages its owner once
options.con: The map must be accurate and up to date

options.name: By machine learning on alert patterns
options.pro: Can find links no one wrote down
options.con: Hard to explain when it is wrong, and it needs history to learn from

alternatives.pick: Service and time window first, then the dependency map as it becomes reliable, always with a manual merge and split.

roles.description: Responders and the customers who subscribe to updates.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: Monitoring tools, the chat bridge, phone and SMS, and the status page.

roles.label: Pager and queues
roles.description: Page jobs with deadlines and the status fan-out.

roles.label: Engine and automation
roles.description: Grouping, escalation and the runbook runner.

roles.label: State
roles.description: Incident store, timeline, postmortems and the standby copy.
